title: Paige Pullen on "The Canon" and Special Education
author: John Lloyd and Paige C. Pullen
summary: In this interview conducted for Special Education Today, John Lloyd questions literacy researcher Paige Pullen about her 2026 book The Canon of Literacy: A Three Sciences Framework, which proposes a shared standard for evaluating reading instruction across three domains: literacy science (what to teach), learning science (how working memory and cumulative practice shape retention), and instructional science (which delivery practices, like modeling and guided practice, reliably work). Pullen traces the book's intellectual debt to special education directly, noting that foundational reading-science concepts like the simple view of reading originated in a special education journal and that Direct Instruction was developed and validated with struggling readers before the wider field adopted it. She turns the argument back on her own field in the interview's most pointed section, arguing special education often gets instructional delivery right while getting content sequencing wrong, and specifically flags cognitive overload, piling the most content onto students who are already behind, as the discipline's central unaddressed weakness. She situates the book against Jeanne Chall's and Marilyn Jager Adams's earlier landmark literacy syntheses, arguing the science of reading was already settled by Adams in 1990 but that the field's failure has been one of synthesis and enforcement, not further research, which is what her three-part 'measuring rod' is designed to provide.
points: The book's central diagnostic tool, the three-sciences framework (literacy science, learning science, instructional science), gives practitioners a specific question to ask when a lesson fails: was the content wrong, the cognitive load too high, or the delivery method ineffective?

Pullen traces a specific historical debt from mainstream reading science to special education: the simple view of reading, now foundational to literacy instruction broadly, was originally published in the special education journal Remedial and Special Education (Gough & Tunmer, 1986).

Her critique of special education's own practice is concrete and self-critical: she has 'literally seen districts require three different programs for different tiers of instruction' instead of intensifying existing instruction through pacing, group size, and frequency, adding cognitive load rather than reducing it for students already behind.

She distinguishes intensification (moving pacing, explicitness, and practice-frequency levers based on real-time student data) from the common misreading of intensification as simply adding more minutes or swapping in a different program.

Pullen positions The Canon's purpose as fundamentally different from Chall's and Adams's earlier syntheses: those books aimed to inform the field, while hers is explicitly designed to be used as an enforceable standard for teacher preparation programs, state mandates, and district curriculum adoption.
quotes: Our field has five decades of reading research and no shared standard, which is how "evidence-based" ends up stamped on two practices that contradict each other. In the area of literacy, educators are data-rich and synthesis-poor.
A great deal of what we now call the science of reading was learned from children who struggled to read.
Direct Instruction was built and tested with the children the system was failing, and it became a mainstay of special education before the wider field rediscovered it.
A student who is behind is usually the student we ask to hold the most at once, because we are trying to make up ground. Working memory does not grant an exception for urgency.
I have literally seen districts require three different programs for different tiers of instruction, rather than intensifying the instruction through pacing, group size, duration, and frequency.
An IEP has to be determined by data and delivered in the least restrictive environment, and that is not aspiration; it is the law and the daily practice.
Adams told us in 1990 what children need to learn about print. We are still arguing about it in 2026. The science settled; the field never did.
